pages.text: A thin man stands at your gate with a ledger under his arm. He does not smile, and he does not look unkind either. He looks like someone who counts. “Master Quill,” he says. “The Lord's steward.”
“The old farm smokes again,” he says, and looks at your chimney. “The Lord wishes to know why.” You tell him: because somebody lives here. He writes that down.
Quill counts everything. Cows, sacks, windows, nails. He counts the hens twice, because one moved. Every number goes into his ledger, written with a very sharp pencil.
Later you find two ledger pages folded into a paper boat on the pond. Somewhere, a very small bell tinkles. Quill is not amused. You are, a little.

c4_lease.title: The old lease
c4_lease.text: In a rusty tin under the glasshouse stones lies the old lease: “… a half of all that the land gives.” A half! You take out the burnt page from the workshop and hold it beside it. The red number is the same.

pages.text: Quill is at the gate again. “The Lord's share,” he says, “as before.” You look at the North Field, resting under clover. “No,” you say. Your voice is smaller than you hoped, but it does not shake.
Quill's pencil stops. On the fence, Lark swings his legs. “You've counted the cows,” he tells Quill. “Have you counted the clover? It counts you.” Quill writes that down too, by mistake.

c4_library.title: Sorted by weight
c4_library.text: You step into the new library room and stop. Somebody has sorted all your books by weight. The heaviest lies at the bottom, the lightest on top. Lark sits on the heaviest, reading the lightest. “Probably fine,” he says.

c4_pizza.title: Pizza night
c4_pizza.text: On the village square the builders eat pizza at long tables under paper lanterns. You sit between Bo and Greenstem. Someone passes you the biggest slice. Tonight, nobody asks whose family you are.

pages.text: A pony stands at your gate and poses, one hoof forward, as if somebody were painting her. Then she lets you load a sack, a crate and a very large order for Hazelwood. She walks down the road as if she owns it.

On the village square, people stop. They look at the pony, then at the order, then at you. Somebody says your name. Your own name, not your family's. And the fourth line comes back: “Strong pony brings the world its bread.”

c4_quill_out.title: Quill rides home
c4_quill_out.text: Quill rides back to the manor with his ledger full. At the gate he stops. “The farm gives back more than it takes,” he says, as if it were a question. “The Lord will want to know.” Then he goes, and you cannot tell what he meant.

pages.text: “Was the Lord a villain?” asks Minena. You think about it for a long time. “He was afraid,” you say. “That's worse, sometimes.”
Nobody says anything. Then the smallest one whispers, “Afraid of what?” “Of a number,” you say. “Now go to sleep.” They do not. Not yet.
